Revised read incorporating the Financial Stability Report and the January 2019 Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS): The March 20, 2019 FOMC statement signals a data-dependent pause with “patience,” citing strong labor markets alongside slower activity, muted inflation, and low market-based inflation compensation. The Financial Stability Report (FSR) tempers the tone with elevated business leverage, stretched valuations, and the risk that compressed risk premiums could widen if growth slows, while funding risks remain moderate.

The SLOOS adds a clearer headwind from credit conditions: banks reported and/or expected tighter standards for C&I loans and construction/land development (CRE), wider loan rate spreads and tighter other terms, and weaker loan demand across business categories and several household segments (including residential real estate and HELOCs). While some categories remained unchanged (e.g., GSE-eligible mortgages, HELOCs, autos), banks anticipated tighter standards through 2019 and deterioration in mortgage and nonprime consumer loan performance, with collateral-value concerns cited as a reason for tightening. These survey insights point to a modest tightening in credit supply and softer loan demand that could restrain growth at the margin and reinforce the FSR’s vulnerability narrative.

Balance-sheet reinvestments and IOER within the floor system still support money market control and keep longer yields supportive, but, on net, the SLOOS tilts the assessment away from “slightly positive” toward neutral-to-slightly negative. The “patient” stance remains appropriate, with downside risks to the outlook incrementally higher due to tightening bank credit and weaker loan demand.
